title_en: 2026 amendment of the Industrial Accident Compensation Insurance Act and related acts

instruments.number: 令和八年法律第六十号
instruments.name_ja: 労働者災害補償保険法等の一部を改正する法律
instruments.name_en: Act Partially Amending the Industrial Accident Compensation Insurance Act and Other Acts

paragraphs: Industrial Accident Compensation Insurance (rousai hoken) pays benefits to workers injured or made ill at work, and to their bereaved families. The Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW) explains that, in view of changes in the employment structure such as greater participation of women in work and more diverse ways of working, the amendment aims to build a broader safety net against occupational accidents.

Under the amendment, a husband no longer has to be aged 60 or over, or in a disability state specified by ministerial ordinance, to be eligible as a bereaved family member for survivors' compensation pensions; that requirement applied only to husbands. Where there is one bereaved family member, the pension amount becomes uniformly 175 days of the benefit base daily amount, abolishing a special amount that applied to a wife aged 55 or over or with a specified disability. Corresponding changes are made to special survivors' pensions under the Act on Asbestos Health Damage Relief.

The amendment also sets out in the Act the requirements for organisations through which self-employed persons and others join the insurance under 'special enrolment', and allows the government to order such organisations to improve their operations and to end the insurance relationship if an order is breached. The limitation period for claiming benefits is extended from two to five years for diseases, specified by Cabinet Order, for which it is not easy to judge whether they are work-related; the Labour Standards Act is amended to match. A provisional measure under which businesses specified by Cabinet Order are, for the time being, not compulsorily covered by the insurance is abolished.

The Cabinet submitted the bill to the Diet on 7 April 2026. It was examined by the Committee on Health, Labour and Welfare of each House, passed by the House of Representatives on 2 June 2026 and by the House of Councillors on 10 July 2026, which enacted it. It was promulgated on 17 July 2026 as Act No. 60 of 2026.

On the day of promulgation the MHLW Labour Standards Bureau issued a notice to prefectural labour bureaus explaining the content and effective dates, and stated that the Cabinet Orders and ministerial ordinances needed for implementation will be considered while hearing the views of labour, management and other parties.

confirmed.text: The Act's main provisions take effect, as stated in the Act's supplementary provisions and recorded by e-Gov Law Search.

Certain provisions took effect on promulgation. The abolition of the provisional non-coverage measure and some other provisions take effect on a date set by Cabinet Order within five years of promulgation.
The Act requires the government to review how the amended acts are working after five years from their entry into force and to take necessary measures based on the results.

expected: Cabinet Orders and ministerial ordinances to implement the amendment are normally discussed with the relevant councils and published in draft for public comment before adoption.
uncertainties: Which diseases will qualify for the five-year limitation period depends on a Cabinet Order that had not been made when this explainer was verified.
The ministerial ordinance requirements for special enrolment organisations had not been published when this explainer was verified.
The date on which the provisional non-coverage measure ends has not been set; it can be no later than five years after promulgation.

paragraphs: The main changes alter the benefits that the insurance pays and who may receive them, rather than creating new reporting duties for most employers. Employers may wish to reflect the new survivor eligibility rules in HR information given to employees and in any company benefit schemes that refer to the statutory benefits.

Organisations that operate special enrolment for self-employed persons, such as associations of sole contractors, will have statutory requirements to meet and may be subject to improvement orders. Businesses that currently fall under the provisional non-coverage measure should follow the Cabinet Order that ends it, since compulsory coverage would bring premium and procedural obligations.
checklist: Update HR guidance on survivors' benefits and on the limitation period for claims.
If you engage self-employed persons who join through special enrolment organisations, note that those organisations will be subject to statutory requirements.
Check whether any part of your business is currently outside compulsory coverage under the provisional measure, and follow the Cabinet Order that will end it.
Watch MHLW for draft Cabinet Orders and ministerial ordinances and their public comment periods.
